text_blocks.snippet: If you test positive for COVID-19, focus on rest, hydration, and symptom management. Over-the-counter medications can help with fever and other discomforts. If your symptoms worsen or you have underlying health conditions, contact a healthcare provider promptly, as treatment may need to be started within 5-7 days of symptom onset according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention | CDC (.gov).
snippet_highlighted_words: focus on rest, hydration, and symptom management

list.snippet: Stay home: Avoid contact with others to prevent the spread of the virus.
Separate yourself: If possible, stay in a separate room and use a separate bathroom from other household members.
Wear a mask: If you must be around others, wear a high-quality mask (like an N95).
Inform close contacts: Let anyone you've been in close contact with recently know about your positive test.
Rest: Get plenty of sleep to allow your body to recover.
Hydration: Drink plenty of fluids, such as water, clear broths, or electrolyte drinks.
Over-the-counter medications: Use medications like acetaminophen or ibuprofen to reduce fever and pain.
Cough and congestion relief: Consider using cough drops, saline nasal spray, or a humidifier.

list.title: Worsening symptoms:
list.snippet: If you experience shortness of breath, persistent chest pain, difficulty staying awake, confusion, or bluish lips or face, seek immediate medical attention.

list.title: Underlying health conditions:
list.snippet: If you have a chronic illness or are immunocompromised, contact your doctor promptly, as you may be eligible for antiviral medications.

list.title: Consult your doctor:
list.snippet: Even if your symptoms are mild, it's a good idea to consult with your doctor or a healthcare professional to determine the best course of action for your specific situation.
Keep track: Note the severity and duration of your symptoms.
Be aware of changes: Report any new or worsening symptoms to your doctor.
CDC recommendations: Follow the latest guidance from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) regarding when it is safe to end isolation says the CDC.
